section.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Brain Tumor Treatment in China: Tiantan Hospital Beijing and the Shanghai Proton Center
section.intro: These FAQs explain how international patients explore brain tumor treatment in China, including Beijing Tiantan Hospital and the Shanghai Proton and Heavy Ion Center. All treatment decisions depend on individual diagnosis and specialist review.

groups.title: Understanding Brain Tumor Treatment in China

items.q: What is brain tumor treatment in China like at Tiantan Hospital and the Shanghai Proton Center?
items.a: Brain tumor treatment in China combines advanced neurosurgery, radiotherapy, and particle therapy at high-volume centers. Beijing Tiantan Hospital is one of the world's largest dedicated neurosurgery institutions, handling many complex brain tumor operations each year. The Shanghai Proton and Heavy Ion Center offers proton and carbon-ion radiotherapy for selected tumors. The right approach depends on tumor type, location, grade, and specialist review by the treating team.

items.q: Why is Beijing Tiantan Hospital well known for brain tumor surgery?
items.a: Beijing Tiantan Hospital is recognized as a leading neurosurgery center because of its very high surgical volume and specialized brain tumor teams. It manages a wide range of conditions, including gliomas, meningiomas, pituitary tumors, and skull base tumors, often using image-guided and awake surgery techniques. High case volume can support surgical experience, but outcomes still depend on the individual tumor, its location, and the patient's overall health.

items.q: What is proton and heavy-ion therapy at the Shanghai Proton Center?
items.a: Proton and heavy-ion therapy are advanced forms of radiotherapy that target tumors while limiting dose to nearby healthy brain tissue. The Shanghai Proton and Heavy Ion Center delivers proton and carbon-ion beams, which may be considered for certain brain and skull base tumors where precision matters. Suitability depends on tumor type, size, location, and prior treatment, and should be confirmed by a radiation oncology team.

items.q: Which types of brain tumors are treated in China?
items.a: Chinese centers treat a broad range of brain tumors, including gliomas, glioblastoma, meningiomas, pituitary adenomas, acoustic neuromas, medulloblastomas, and skull base tumors. Both benign and malignant tumors may be managed, along with brain metastases from other cancers. The chosen treatment—surgery, radiotherapy, particle therapy, chemotherapy, or a combination—depends on the specific diagnosis, tumor grade, molecular features, and an assessment by the treating oncology and neurosurgery team.

items.q: Who may be eligible for proton or heavy-ion therapy for a brain tumor?
items.a: Proton or heavy-ion therapy may be suitable for selected patients whose tumor location and type benefit from highly focused radiation. It is often considered for tumors near critical structures, some skull base tumors, and certain pediatric cases where reducing dose to healthy tissue is important. Eligibility depends on tumor type, stage, previous treatment, and overall health, and final decisions should be made by the treating radiation oncology team.

items.q: How does the treatment process usually work for international patients?
items.a: The process usually begins with a remote review of medical records, imaging, and pathology by the hospital's specialists. If the case appears suitable, the center provides a treatment plan and estimated cost, followed by travel and admission. After arrival, patients typically undergo repeat imaging and evaluation before surgery or radiotherapy begins. The exact steps depend on tumor type and the treating team's assessment after in-person review.

items.q: Is brain tumor surgery in China safe?
items.a: Brain tumor surgery at experienced centers uses modern techniques such as neuronavigation, intraoperative imaging, and awake mapping to help protect brain function. However, all brain surgery carries risks, including bleeding, infection, swelling, seizures, and neurological changes. The level of risk depends on tumor location, size, and the patient's condition. Potential benefits and risks should be discussed in detail with the qualified neurosurgical team before any procedure.

items.q: What medical reports are needed to plan treatment?
items.a: Centers generally need recent brain MRI or CT scans, pathology or biopsy reports if available, previous surgical and treatment summaries, and a list of current medications. Molecular or genetic test results, blood work, and details of overall health also help specialists assess the case. Complete, up-to-date reports allow a more accurate opinion, but the final plan is confirmed only after in-person evaluation by the treating team.

items.q: How much does brain tumor treatment in China cost?
items.a: Costs vary widely depending on tumor type, the procedures required, and length of stay. Neurosurgery, proton therapy, and heavy-ion therapy each have different price ranges, and complex cases usually cost more. Final cost depends on the hospital, diagnosis, stage, tests, treatment protocol, complications, and treating team advice. Patients should request a written estimate before travel and treat any figure as approximate until confirmed by the hospital.

items.q: How does the cost compare with other countries?
items.a: Brain tumor treatment costs in China may be lower than in the United States or parts of Europe for some patients, but this is not guaranteed and varies by case. Particle therapy in particular can be expensive anywhere it is offered. Comparing countries should account for treatment quality, waiting times, travel, accommodation, and follow-up. A reliable comparison is only possible after each center reviews the individual diagnosis and provides an estimate.

items.q: How can international patients access Tiantan Hospital or the Shanghai Proton Center?
items.a: International patients usually access these centers by submitting medical records for remote review through the hospital's international patient services or a coordinating organization. If the case is accepted, the center advises on scheduling, cost, and travel. Access depends on hospital acceptance, medical review, visa approval, and travel fitness. No center can guarantee admission or a specific treatment, and each case is assessed individually before any commitment is made.

items.q: Which countries offer proton and heavy-ion therapy besides China?
items.a: Proton and heavy-ion therapy are available in several countries, including the United States, Japan, Germany, and others, in addition to China. Heavy-ion (carbon-ion) therapy is offered at fewer centers worldwide, which is why some patients travel for it. The best option depends on tumor type, availability, waiting times, cost, and specialist recommendation. A qualified radiation oncology team should confirm whether particle therapy is appropriate for a given case.

items.q: Are clinical trials for brain tumors available in China?
items.a: Clinical trials for brain tumors, including gliomas and glioblastoma, are conducted at some Chinese centers and may explore new drugs, immunotherapy, or combined approaches. Participation is not guaranteed and does not guarantee benefit. Eligibility is decided only after medical record review and investigator assessment, and trials often have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Patients interested in a trial should discuss options carefully with their treating oncology team.

items.q: What advanced technologies are used for brain tumor treatment in China?
items.a: Advanced technologies used at major Chinese centers may include neuronavigation, intraoperative MRI, awake craniotomy with brain mapping, stereotactic radiosurgery, and proton or heavy-ion radiotherapy. Some centers also use molecular testing to guide treatment. These tools can support precision, but they do not suit every tumor or patient. Whether a specific technology is appropriate depends on the diagnosis and the judgment of the treating specialist team.

items.q: Is particle therapy better than standard radiotherapy for brain tumors?
items.a: Particle therapy is not automatically better than standard radiotherapy; it may be advantageous for selected tumors where sparing nearby healthy tissue is important. For many brain tumors, conventional radiotherapy or surgery remains highly effective and appropriate. The best choice depends on tumor type, location, grade, and overall health. A radiation oncology team should weigh the potential benefits and limitations before recommending particle therapy over standard options.

items.q: Do international patients need a visa and how long is the stay?
items.a: International patients typically need a medical or appropriate travel visa to receive treatment in China, and hospitals may provide supporting documents for the application. Length of stay depends on whether surgery, radiotherapy, or particle therapy is planned, and on recovery and follow-up needs. Visa approval, hospital admission, and travel fitness cannot be guaranteed. Patients should plan for possible extensions and confirm requirements with official sources before travelling.

items.q: Is a second opinion recommended before traveling for brain tumor treatment?
items.a: A second opinion is often recommended before traveling for brain tumor treatment, as it can confirm the diagnosis and clarify whether surgery, radiotherapy, or particle therapy is appropriate. Reviewing scans and pathology with more than one specialist may help patients understand their options and risks. Final treatment decisions should be made by the treating medical team, ideally after the patient's full records and imaging have been carefully reviewed.

items.q: How is follow-up care handled after returning home?
items.a: Follow-up care after brain tumor treatment usually involves regular imaging, symptom monitoring, and sometimes ongoing medication or rehabilitation, often coordinated with doctors in the patient's home country. Treating centers may provide discharge summaries and imaging to support continuity of care. The follow-up schedule depends on tumor type, treatment received, and recovery. Patients should arrange local oncology or neurosurgical follow-up and discuss any new symptoms promptly with their medical team.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with brain tumor treatment in China?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centers, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health. CancerFax does not replace doctors or hospitals and cannot guarantee hospital admission, visa approval, or any particular treatment outcome.
